porbos.title: The Proposal to Dig a Trench • Days of Hunger • Jabir’s Hospitality • The Night of Fear

blocks.0: The Proposal to Dig a Trench
blocks.1: Banu al-Nadir, expelled, had taken refuge in Khaybar. From there they went first to Makkah, to Quraysh; since the account of Badr and Uhud was still unsettled, Quraysh readily agreed. Then Banu al-Nadir went to Ghatafan with the same call, promising to stand beside them themselves. On learning that Quraysh had agreed, Ghatafan agreed too. An army of about ten thousand, including Quraysh, Ghatafan, Banu Asad and Banu Sulaym, set out toward Madinah. This combined army is called al-Ahzab, the confederates.{{1}}
blocks.2: On receiving the news the Prophet {{1}} sat in consultation with the Companions. Salman al-Farisi (RA) said, in Persia when we feared an enemy, we used to dig a trench around the city. The Arabs had never seen this tactic before. The Prophet {{2}} accepted the proposal.{{3}}
blocks.3: One suggestion from a foreign Companion changed Arabia’s whole way of war. The Prophet {{1}} had not shut the door to learning something new, looking not only at who is speaking but at whether the idea is useful. The north of Madinah was open, the other sides were enclosed by mountains and houses. To every ten Companions was given the duty of digging forty cubits. The Prophet {{2}} himself also dug earth, carried earth on his shoulder, so that the dust covered even the hair of his belly.{{3}}
blocks.4: Those who finished their own portion early did not sit with folded hands; they ran to help with others’ unfinished sections. This trench, three and a half miles long, was completed in this way in six days.{{1}}
blocks.5: One could have finished one’s own portion and sat with folded hands; no one would have said anything. But winning as a team and completing one’s own duty alone are not the same. While carrying earth he would recite, in the rhythm of ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah (RA),
blocks.7: O Allah, were it not for You we would not have been guided, nor given charity, nor prayed. Send down tranquillity upon us, keep our feet firm when we meet them; they have transgressed against us, and if they want fitnah, we refuse.{{1}}
blocks.8: When a leader carries earth with his own hands and stands beside his followers, the order is not only in words. ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (RA) used to say,
blocks.10: On the day of Uhud I was presented before the Prophet {{1}}, I was fourteen then; he did not permit me. On the day of the Trench I was presented again, I was fifteen then; he permitted me. Nafi‘ (RA) used to say, later I went to ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz, he was then caliph, and told him this hadith; he said, this is indeed the boundary between the young and the grown. Then he wrote to all his officials that whoever has completed fifteen years should be counted as an adult.{{2}}
blocks.11: The same boy, a year’s gap; the first time sent back, the second time given a place in the fighting ranks. The Prophet {{1}} neither pushed anyone into risk without preparation, nor kept anyone back when he saw them prepared. Years later this same hadith reached, through Nafi‘ (RA), the caliph ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz, may Allah have mercy on him; he made it state policy, treating fifteen years as the boundary between young and grown, writing to all officials. This is one example of how the testimony of one event becomes law many years later.
blocks.13: A freezing morning. Muhajirun and Ansar were digging earth together, carrying it on their shoulders. There were no slaves to do this work; they did everything themselves. Seeing their fatigue and hunger the Prophet {{1}} made du‘a,
blocks.15: O Allah, the real life is the life of the Hereafter; forgive the Ansar and the Muhajirun.{{1}}
blocks.18: We are the ones who pledged allegiance to Muhammad for jihad, for as long as we live.{{1}}
blocks.19: One makes du‘a for forgiveness, the other replies with a pledge. No one is asking anything of anyone; both are giving. The food was a little barley flour, the bread made of it bitter and foul-smelling, yet even that was shared among the hungry people.{{1}}
blocks.20: In the middle of digging a hard rock came up, the pickaxe was breaking, the earth was not breaking. Jabir (RA) used to say,
blocks.22: We were digging on the day of the Trench, and a hard rock came up. The Companions came to the Prophet {{1}} and said, a rocky patch has come up in the trench. He said, I am coming down. Then he stood up, his belly tied with a stone; we had not tasted any food for three days. The Prophet {{2}} took the pickaxe in his hand, struck, and the rock became like loose sand.{{3}}
blocks.23: In one narration, with each strike Salman (RA) saw a flash of light. When asked, the Prophet {{1}} said, with the first strike he was shown the palaces of Sham, with the second Persia’s al-Mada’in, with the third the gates of San‘a’; he gave the good news that victory would come in all three directions.{{2}}
blocks.24: In the darkest moment of hunger and fatigue the farthest good news seemed to arrive. Through hardship we see the light of the future, not by avoiding hardship. Abu Talhah (RA) used to say,
blocks.26: We complained of hunger to the Prophet {{1}}, and we had each tied a stone to our belly; the Prophet {{2}} lifted two stones from his belly and showed us.{{3}}
blocks.27: To be a leader means to be the hungriest, to bear hardship first.
blocks.29: Seeing this intense hunger of the Prophet {{1}}, the heart of Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA) was stirred. At home there was only one sa‘ of barley, about three and a half kilos by today’s measure. He used to say,
blocks.31: When the trench was dug, I saw intense hunger in the Prophet {{1}}. I went to my wife and asked, do you have anything? I have seen intense hunger in the Prophet {{2}}. She brought out a bag, in it a sa‘ of barley; and we had a tame young goat, I slaughtered it, my wife ground the barley, she finished when I finished; I put the meat in the pot in pieces. Then I went back to the Prophet {{3}}. My wife said, do not disgrace me before the Prophet {{4}} and his companions. I went to him and whispered, O Messenger of Allah, we have slaughtered a young goat of ours, and ground a sa‘ of barley that we had at home; come, with a few men. The Prophet {{5}} asked, how much? I said, I told him how much. He said, a lot, good; tell her, do not take the pot down, nor take the bread from the oven, until I come. Then he said, rise. The Muhajirun and Ansar stood up.{{6}}
blocks.32: Jabir (RA) then ran to his wife and said, disaster! The Prophet {{1}} is coming with all the Muhajirun and Ansar! His wife only said, did he ask how much there is? Jabir (RA) said, yes. The Prophet {{2}} entered the house and said, come in, do not crowd. Then he himself was breaking the bread, putting meat on it, covering the pot, covering the oven, delivering to everyone as much as he took out. In this way the breaking and handing out of bread went on until everyone ate their fill. Still food remained in the pot and the oven.{{3}}
blocks.33: One sa‘ of barley, one young goat. Several hundred people ate, Muhajirun and Ansar together, yet it did not run out. For the hand that gives blessing, the reckoning of little and much is not like people’s reckoning.
blocks.35: As soon as the digging of the trench around Madinah was finished, the huge army of the Ahzab came and surrounded it. The Prophet {{1}} came out with the Companions, put his back toward Mount Sal‘, put the trench between themselves and the enemy; against ten thousand only three thousand Companions.{{2}}
blocks.36: Huyayy ibn Akhtab, the expelled leader of Banu al-Nadir, then ran to Ka‘b ibn Asad, the leader of Banu Qurayzah, whose security pact with the Prophet {{1}} was still in force. Ka‘b, on hearing the news, shut the door of his fortress in Huyayy’s face. Huyayy called, open the door. Ka‘b said, you are an ill-omened man; I have made a pact with Muhammad, I have found nothing from him but honesty and faithfulness, I will not break this pact. Huyayy said, are you keeping the door shut in fear that I will share even a meal of yours? Angered by this, Ka‘b opened the door. Huyayy said, I have brought you the greatest force of the age, an army like a flood; Quraysh has come with its leaders, Ghatafan too with its leaders; they have promised not to return until they wipe out Muhammad and his companions. Ka‘b said, you have brought a cloud of disgrace, thundering within, with no rain; spare me, I have seen nothing from Muhammad but honesty and faithfulness. Huyayy still persisted, kept saying the same thing again and again, in the end Ka‘b agreed on the condition that if Quraysh and Ghatafan returned unable to do anything to Muhammad, Huyayy would take shelter with him in his fortress, whatever came upon him would come upon Huyayy too. In this way Ka‘b broke the pact.{{2}}
blocks.37: When the news reached the Prophet {{1}}, he sent Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA) (leader of the Aws), Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubadah (RA) (leader of the Khazraj), ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah (RA) and Khawwat ibn Jubayr (RA) to verify. He said, see whether the news is true; if true, tell by hint, do not break people’s morale; if false, say it openly. They went and saw that Banu Qurayzah were saying openly insulting words, denying even the Messenger of Allah {{2}}. Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA) cursed them, they came back and told by hint, the news is true. The Prophet {{3}} said, Allahu Akbar, take the good news, O Muslims.{{4}}
blocks.38: The Muslims were caught in a siege from two sides, enemies front and back. The Qur’an describes this moment thus,
blocks.40: Remember when they came upon you from above and from below, and when eyes were bulging and hearts rose to the throats, and you began to think various thoughts about Allah. Then the believers were severely tested and were shaken with a violent shaking.{{1}}
blocks.41: ‘A’ishah (RA) used to say, this verse is about the day of the Trench.{{1}}
blocks.42: Excitement, siege, fear of treachery inside our own home; when fear reaches such a limit, then it is known how deeply someone’s faith is set. ‘Ali (RA) used to say, on the day of the Trench the enemies kept us so busy that we could not pray the middle prayer, ‘Asr, until the sun set. The Prophet {{1}} said, may Allah fill their houses and graves with fire, as they kept us busy from the middle prayer.{{2}}
blocks.43: The Prophet {{1}} made du‘a again and again against the enemies,
blocks.45: O Allah, Revealer of the Book, swift in reckoning, defeat the Confederates. O Allah, defeat them, shake them.{{1}}
blocks.46: One day ‘Umar (RA) came, cursing the disbelievers of Quraysh, and said, O Messenger of Allah, the sun almost set while I was praying ‘Asr. The Prophet {{1}} said, by Allah, I have not prayed it either. Then they went to Buthan, made wudu’, prayed ‘Asr after sunset, then Maghrib.{{2}}
blocks.47: A person who is himself tired, hungry, surrounded by danger, yet is most pained by a prayer slipping away, nothing more is needed to understand where his priority lay.

footnotes.0: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-Khandaq aw al-Ahzab’ (the instigation of Banu al-Nadir, the formation of the combined army). Sirah-based.
footnotes.1: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-Khandaq’ (the proposal of Salman al-Farisi (RA)). Sirah-based.
footnotes.2: Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa al-Muluk (through Qudamah ibn ‘Abdillah ibn ‘Amr al-Muzani, the account of the division of forty cubits per ten men). Sirah-based.
footnotes.3: Ma‘arif al-Qur’an (Mufti Muhammad Shafi‘; English edition), vol. 7, introductory part of Surah al-Ahzab, pp. 112–113 (quoted through al-Qurtubi and al-Mazhari).
footnotes.4: Sahih al-Bukhari 4106 (from al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA), through Abu Ishaq); in close wording also in Sahih al-Bukhari 4108–4110.
footnotes.7: Sahih al-Bukhari 4099, 4100 (from Anas ibn Malik (RA), through two different chains, close narrations of the same event)
footnotes.10: Imam al-Bayhaqi, Dala’il al-Nubuwwah (from al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA) through Maymun ibn Astadh) ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah. Ibn Kathir himself wrote ‘hadithun gharibun, tafarrada bihi Maymun ibn Astadh’ (this is a gharib hadith narrated through a single chain). There are three more different narrations on the same subject through various chains (al-Nasa’i: Persia-Rome-Abyssinia, through an unknown Companion; al-Tabarani: Persia-Rome-Himyar, through the weak narrator ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad ibn An‘um; al-Tabarani-Ibn ‘Abbas: Sham-Persia), each weak or gharib in chain, none sahih. In the detailed lists of cities of conquest there are also discrepancies among the narrations themselves.
footnotes.11: Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 2371; Shama’il al-Tirmidhi 134 (from Abu Talhah (RA), through Sayyar ibn Hatim ← Sahl ibn Aslam ← Yazid ibn Abi Mansur ← Anas ibn Malik (RA)). Imam al-Tirmidhi himself called it ‘gharib, I do not know it except through this one chain’; later muhaddithun (the al-Albani/‘Ali Za’i line) called it hasan. The wording of the hadith does not directly contain ‘on the day of the Trench’; the Sirah tradition, according to context, joins it to the account of the hunger of the Trench, and the dars also uses it that way.
footnotes.14: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Fasl Nuzul Quraysh’ (the Muslim army three thousand, back toward Mount Sal‘). Sirah-based.
footnotes.15: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Fasl Nuzul Quraysh bi-Mujtama‘ al-Asyal Yawm al-Khandaq’ (the full conversation of Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka‘b ibn Asad, Banu Qurayzah’s breach of pact). Sirah-based.
footnotes.16: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Fasl Nuzul Quraysh’ (the delegation of Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh, Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubadah, ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah and Khawwat ibn Jubayr (RA)). Sirah-based.
footnotes.17: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 3, Surah al-Ahzab 33:10–11, p. 71 (Taqi ‘Uthmani; checked against the rendered PDF).
footnotes.19: Sahih al-Bukhari 4111 (from ‘Ali (RA)); in Sahih al-Bukhari 4112 ‘Umar (RA)’s narration of the same event, with the account of going to Buthan and making up the prayer.
footnotes.21: Sahih al-Bukhari 4112 (from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA), narrating the event of ‘Umar (RA)).

porbos.title: The Excuses of the Hypocrites • The Peace Proposal to Ghatafan • Single Combat • Safiyyah’s Courage • Sa‘d’s Wound • Nu‘aym’s Diplomacy

blocks.1: The longer the siege dragged on, the clearer the cracks inside became. The hypocrites and the weak in faith were looking for excuses to go back. Mu‘attib ibn Qushayr of Banu ‘Amr ibn ‘Awf had said, Muhammad used to promise us that we would eat the treasures of Kisra and Qaysar, yet today not one of us can even go to the toilet safely. Aws ibn Qayzi had said, O Messenger of Allah, our houses are exposed before the enemy; give us permission, let us go back.{{1}}
blocks.2: The Qur’an has put these words of the hypocrites like this,
blocks.4: And remember when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease were saying, what Allah and His Messenger promised us is nothing but deception. And when a group of them said, O people of Yathrib! There is no place for you here, so go back; and a party of them were asking the Prophet for permission (to go home), saying, our houses are exposed, whereas they were not exposed; rather, their intention was only to flee (by some means).{{1}}
blocks.5: An excuse that sounds beautiful on the tongue often hides only the wish to run from fear. The house is not exposed, the heart is exposed. The Qur’an has told their real condition like this,
blocks.7: If the enemies had entered upon them from all sides of Madinah and they had been asked to join the rebellion, they would surely have joined it, and would have stayed in their homes only a little.{{1}}
blocks.8: There was another group, of whom the Qur’an speaks like this,
blocks.10: (And that too) grudging toward you. So when danger comes, you will see them looking at you with eyes rolling, like one fainting from fear of death. Then when the danger passes, they lash you with sharp tongues out of greed for wealth. They never believed. So Allah has made their deeds worthless, and that is very easy for Allah.{{1}}
blocks.11: The same people, cowardly before the battle and greedy before the spoils; both are symptoms of the same disease, a deficit of faith. Set against this flight of the hypocrites, the Qur’an has stood up a measure, saying,
blocks.13: Indeed, in the Messenger there is for you an excellent example; for one who hopes in Allah and the Day of the Hereafter and remembers Allah much.{{1}}
blocks.14: For the one who looks for excuses, there are a thousand ways to flee. For the one who takes the Messenger as the example, there is only one way, forward.
blocks.16: The siege had gone on for nearly a month, and apart from the exchange of arrows there had been no major clash. When people were in pain from hardship, the Prophet {{1}} sent men to two leaders of Ghatafan, ‘Uyaynah ibn Hisn and al-Harith ibn ‘Awf, with a proposal: he would give one-third of Madinah’s dates, in return for their going back with their people. Talks moved forward, and a document was almost drawn up as well, though the final signing had not yet taken place.{{2}}
blocks.17: Before deciding, the Prophet {{1}} called the two Sa‘ds for consultation. They asked, is this a command from Allah, or your own decision? The Prophet {{2}} said, my own decision; seeing the Arabs pounce on you united, I thought I would break some of their strength. Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA) said,
blocks.19: O Messenger of Allah, when we and these people were upon shirk, we did not know Allah; even then they could not eat a single date of ours for nothing, except through sale or as guests. Now that Allah has honoured us with Islam and given us dignity through you, are we to hand our wealth over to them? We have no need of this; by Allah, we will give them nothing but the sword, until Allah decides between us and them.{{1}}
blocks.20: The Prophet {{1}} said, then let it be your decision. Sa‘d (RA) took the document in his hand and erased it. Those who used to bow their heads in the Jahiliyyah, Islam had given those very same people the courage to say no with dignity. Not holding off the enemy with wealth, but fighting by the strength of faith.
blocks.22: Finding no way across the trench, a few horsemen of Quraysh chose a narrow spot, spurred their horses and leapt across to the other side of the Khandaq. ‘Amr ibn ‘Abd Wudd, ‘Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, Hubayrah ibn Abi Wahb, Dirar ibn al-Khattab; four famous warriors came down onto the open ground between the trench and Mount Sal‘. ‘Amr was then one of the most famous warriors of Arabia; having been wounded at Badr he had not been able to take part at Uhud, and this was the first time he had returned to the field. He halted his horse and shouted, who will fight me? No one answered. ‘Ali (RA) stood up and said, O Messenger of Allah, I will. The Prophet {{1}} said, sit down, that is ‘Amr. ‘Amr said mockingly, did you not say that your dead go to Paradise? Then why do you not send even one against me? ‘Ali (RA) stood up again, and the Prophet {{2}} again said, sit down. The third time, when ‘Amr issued the same challenge, ‘Ali (RA) stood up again and said, O Messenger of Allah, I will go, even though he is ‘Amr. This time the Prophet {{3}} permitted. ‘Ali (RA) went close and first said, I call you to Allah, to His Messenger, to Islam. ‘Amr said, I have no need of that. ‘Ali (RA) said, then I call you to single combat.{{4}}
blocks.23: ‘Amr asked, who are you? He said, ‘Ali. ‘Amr said, the son of Abu Talib? He said, yes. ‘Amr said, cousin, among your uncles there are others older than you; I do not want to shed your blood. ‘Ali (RA) replied, by Allah, but I do want to shed yours.{{1}}
blocks.24: Unable to win in words, ‘Amr grew angry, got down from his horse, hamstrung it himself, then leapt at him. A fierce fight followed; ‘Amr struck ‘Ali (RA) on the head and wounded him, ‘Ali (RA) struck at his neck. So much dust rose that from outside one could not tell who had won. The Prophet {{1}} understood from the sound of takbir that ‘Ali (RA) had killed ‘Amr. The other three spurred their horses, crossed the trench and fled. When ‘Ali (RA) came back, ‘Umar (RA) asked, why did you not strip off his armour? There is no better armour in Arabia. ‘Ali (RA) said, when I struck, his private parts were exposed, so I felt ashamed to strip the clothes from the body of a cousin. Later Quraysh sent men wanting to buy ‘Amr’s corpse for a great sum. The Prophet {{2}} said, keep it, we do not eat the price of the dead.{{3}}
blocks.25: A single challenge, a single fight; the moment the greatest warrior of the ten-thousand-strong army was defeated, the rest understood that winning this siege was not going to be easy. Fear lifts only when someone steps forward.
blocks.27: The men able to fight were then in the trench. In the fortresses inside Madinah were the women and children, together with some men assigned to guard them. In Fari‘, the fortress of Hassan ibn Thabit (RA), was Safiyyah bint ‘Abd al-Muttalib (RA), paternal aunt of the Prophet {{1}}; Hassan (RA) was there too, on this very guard duty. A Jewish man began to wander around the fortress. Banu Qurayzah had by then broken the pact; the Prophet {{2}} and the Companions were facing the enemy, with no way to come back. Safiyyah (RA) said to Hassan (RA), this man may see the hidden side of the fortress, he may call more of his own people; go down and kill him. Hassan (RA) said, may Allah forgive you, daughter of ‘Abd al-Muttalib; you know well that this is not my work. Safiyyah (RA) herself took a stick in her hand and went down from the fortress, struck the man and killed him, then came back and said, go down, bring his belongings; only modesty stopped me, because he is a man. Hassan (RA) said, I have no need of his belongings.{{3}}
blocks.28: The men were in the trench then, the women alone in the fortress; yet one woman’s alertness and courage saved the women and children of the whole fortress. ‘Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr (RA) was then a little boy, with the women and children in another fortress. ‘Umar ibn Abi Salamah (RA) was with him too; the two, each climbing on the other’s shoulders, would try to peep over the fortress wall to see how the fighting was going. ‘Abdullah (RA) saw that his father al-Zubayr (RA) was running now this way, now that; wherever there was danger, he was there. In the evening when his father returned, the son said, Father, I saw you today. Al-Zubayr (RA) said, you saw me, my son? Then may my father and mother be sacrificed for you.{{1}}
blocks.29: Even a child far from the battlefield had seen his father’s courage; that very sight perhaps later prepared him for the hardest fights of his own life.
blocks.31: ‘A’ishah (RA) was then in the fortress of Banu Harithah, and Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh’s (RA) mother was there too. One day Sa‘d (RA) was passing by the fortress in battle dress, the sleeves of his armour so short that his whole arm was bare, a spear in his hand, reciting in rhythm: wait a little, the time to see battle has come; when the hour of death comes, there is no harm in death. His mother called from behind, son, go quickly, you are late. ‘A’ishah (RA), seeing him, said, I wished Sa‘d’s armour had been a little longer.{{1}}
blocks.32: This very fear of the mother came true. ‘A’ishah (RA) used to say,
blocks.34: On the day of the Trench Sa‘d (RA) was wounded; a man of Quraysh struck him, who was called Hibban ibn al-‘Ariqah; the arrow pierced the vein of his arm. The Prophet {{1}} pitched a tent in the mosque, to look after him from close by.{{2}}
blocks.35: The arrow had pierced exactly that bare spot of the armour. The one who stands foremost with a weapon in hand is the first to bleed. The Prophet {{1}} kept him before his own eyes, so that there would be no lapse in care. Sa‘d (RA) had made du‘a, O Allah, if You have left any war with Quraysh remaining, keep me alive to fight them; and if this is the last war, make this very wound the occasion of my martyrdom, and do not give me death until my eyes are cooled concerning Banu Qurayzah.{{2}}
blocks.37: Nu‘aym ibn Mas‘ud of the Ghatafan tribe had accepted Islam in secret; his own tribe did not know. He came to the Prophet {{1}} and said, I have become Muslim, my tribe does not know; I will do whatever you say. The Prophet {{2}} said, you are only one man among us; if you can, create division among them, for war is the name of strategy.
blocks.40: Nu‘aym (RA) went first to Banu Qurayzah; in the days of the Jahiliyyah he had been their friend. He said, you know what my relation with you is. Quraysh and Ghatafan are not like you; this city is yours, your wealth, children and wives are all here, you have no way to move elsewhere. Their homes are elsewhere. If they get a chance they will take their gain, if not they will go back to their own land, leaving you alone to face this man; then you will not have the strength to hold him back. So do not enter the war with them without taking some of their leaders as hostages. Then he went to Quraysh and said to Abu Sufyan, the Jews regret their decision, they have sent word to Muhammad asking forgiveness; they have said they will hand over some of your leaders to be killed, and in return join him to finish off the rest. So if the Jews ask for hostages, do not give even one. He said the same thing when he went to Ghatafan too.{{1}}
blocks.41: On Saturday night Quraysh and Ghatafan told Banu Qurayzah, get ready, we will attack together. Banu Qurayzah replied, today is Saturday, we do not work; and we will not fight unless you give hostages. Quraysh and Ghatafan understood that Nu‘aym’s word was true; they refused to give hostages. Banu Qurayzah too understood that Nu‘aym’s word was true, that these people were merely opportunists; they too refused to fight alone.{{1}}
blocks.42: One man, saying three different things in three directions, broke the whole alliance without lying to anyone. Every word was true; only the time and place of speaking were calculated. Once the seed of suspicion is sown, an alliance no longer remains an alliance.

quiz.q: What was Mu‘attib ibn Qushayr essentially complaining about?
o: The extreme lack of food
The weak and short-sighted leadership of the army
The promised treasures of Kisra and Qaysar
A wrong war strategy

quiz.q: What did Aws ibn Qayzi say when asking permission to go back?
o: That he was feeling ill
That there was trouble in the family
That he did not have enough weapons
That the houses were exposed before the enemy
quiz.e: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir; Surah al-Ahzab 33:13.

quiz.q: Why did the Qur’an call the hypocrites’ excuse ‘our houses are exposed’ a lie?
o: The houses were really protected, they only wanted to flee
Because they really had no houses at all
Because they knew there would be no war
Because the Prophet ﷺ had not given permission

quiz.q: Cowardly before battle, greedy before the spoils: this behaviour is a sign of what?
o: A sign of mere lack of courage
A sign of a deficit of faith
A sign of the effect of poverty
A sign of lack of training
quiz.e: In the light of Surah al-Ahzab 33:19.

quiz.q: What can be applied from the hypocrites’ beautiful-sounding excuses?
o: It should be assumed that every excuse given by everyone is true
Giving excuses is never a fault
One should sit in judgment on others’ excuses
One should check the real reason behind each of one’s own excuses

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ want to give Ghatafan in return for peace?
o: Half of Madinah’s land
Some camels and horses
The release of all prisoners of war
One-third of Madinah’s dates

quiz.q: Why did Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA) reject the peace proposal?
o: Because the Prophet ﷺ had forbidden him
Because Ghatafan themselves finally withdrew the whole proposal altogether
Because the time for writing the document had run out
They gave nothing free even in the Jahiliyyah, let alone after Islam

quiz.q: What can be learned about self-respect from Sa‘d’s (RA) rejection?
o: Everything should be given up to keep the enemy happy
After receiving honour, one should not bow the head easily
The leader’s decision should not be questioned
All problems can be solved with wealth

quiz.q: Who stood up against ‘Amr ibn ‘Abd Wudd in single combat?
o: ‘Ali (RA)
‘Umar (RA)
al-Zubayr (RA)
Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA)

quiz.q: After how many times of ‘Amr’s challenge did the Prophet ﷺ permit ‘Ali (RA)?
o: The first time
The third time
The second time
The fourth time

quiz.q: What reason did ‘Ali (RA) give for not taking ‘Amr’s armour?
o: There was no time in the haste of battle
The armour had been torn and ruined by the blow
He felt ashamed because the private parts had been exposed
The Prophet ﷺ had forbidden it

quiz.q: When Quraysh wanted to buy ‘Amr’s corpse, what did the Prophet ﷺ say?
o: They fixed a price for it
The corpse will not be returned
First agreed, then refused
We do not eat the price of the dead

quiz.q: Why did the Prophet ﷺ tell ‘Ali (RA) to sit down the first two times?
o: Because he had little trust in ‘Ali
He wanted to give someone else a chance
Considering ‘Amr’s strength and fame
Because the time had not yet come

quiz.q: Why did ‘Amr’s defeat become a great blow to the whole allied army?
o: Because he was their only soldier
A food crisis arose with his sudden death
Quraysh stopped the war at once
Because he was their most famous warrior

quiz.q: Why did the Prophet ﷺ refuse to take money in exchange for ‘Amr’s corpse?
o: Because taking the price of the dead is against honour
Because the amount of money was small
Because on principle he did not want any dealings with Quraysh
Because ‘Ali (RA) forbade it

quiz.q: What can be learned from ‘Ali (RA) stepping forward even though everyone was silent?
o: One person’s courage can change the whole situation
Stepping forward alone is always a dangerous act
Nothing should be done without the group’s consent
One should not advance without the leader’s permission

quiz.q: What can be learned from ‘Ali’s (RA) sense of shame even at the moment of victory?
o: Respect should not be shown to the enemy
Modesty should not be given up even after victory
When one wins a war, taking everything is natural
For kinship’s sake everything must be given up

quiz.q: Who killed the Jewish man who was wandering around Hassan’s fortress?
o: Safiyyah bint ‘Abd al-Muttalib (RA)
‘Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam (RA)
Hassan ibn Thabit (RA)
‘Umar ibn Abi Salamah (RA)

quiz.q: Why did Safiyyah (RA) not bring down the man’s belongings herself?
o: There was no time to go down
Only out of modesty, because he was a man
She did not dare go down alone
Hassan (RA) forbade her

quiz.q: Why is Safiyyah’s incident important, when the men were all in the trench?
o: It was a rare exception
Even one woman’s alertness can save a whole fortress
Because she was the Prophet’s ﷺ paternal aunt
Merely to prove Hassan’s personal weakness

quiz.q: What can be learned about alertness from Safiyyah’s incident?
o: One should always depend on others in everything
There is no need to think about the defence of women
On seeing danger one can take action oneself
One should attack at the slightest suspicion

quiz.q: What can be learned about child-rearing from the incident of Ibn al-Zubayr seeing his father?
o: Children should always be kept near war
It is improper to question a father’s work
A child should not be praised
An example of good conduct shapes the child

quiz.q: Who shot Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA) with the arrow?
o: Abu Sufyan himself
‘Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl
Hibban ibn al-‘Ariqah
‘Amr ibn ‘Abd Wudd

quiz.q: Why did ‘A’ishah (RA) say she wished Sa‘d’s armour were longer?
o: Because she did not like war
Because Sa‘d himself had requested it
Because she saw danger in the arm left bare by the short sleeves
It was merely a general remark about the beauty of the armour

quiz.q: What can be learned from Sa‘d’s du‘a (if I live I will fight, if not, martyrdom)?
o: One can remain content with Allah’s decision in both situations
Wishing for death is always the greatest and best act
Life has no meaning without war
There is no need to make du‘a when wounded

quiz.q: Why did Nu‘aym’s strategy succeed, although he did not lie?
o: He used weapons
Both sides were already weak
He supposedly bribed both sides separately with plenty of money
By telling the truth at exactly the right time and place he sowed suspicion

quiz.q: What can be learned about conflict resolution from Nu‘aym’s strategy?
o: No talk with the enemy should ever have been held then
Even the truth, said in the right place, can reduce disorder
Strategy means lying
One man cannot change a big situation

porbos.title: The Storm and the Retreat • Jibril’s Command • Sa‘d’s Judgment • Final Word

blocks.1: When the alliance had begun to break apart from within through mutual distrust, Allah sent a stormy night of fierce cold. Pots overturned, tents were uprooted, fires went out.
blocks.3: I have been helped by the east wind, and ‘Ad were destroyed by the west wind.{{1}}
blocks.4: The same wind, two fates. Destruction for one people, help for another; the wind is only a means, the decision is always Allah’s. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (RA) used to say,
blocks.6: We were with the Prophet {{1}} on the night of the Confederates; a fierce storm and bitter cold gripped us. The Prophet {{2}} said, is there anyone who will bring me news of the enemy camp, that Allah will make him my companion on the Day of Resurrection? We kept silent, none of us answered. He said again, the same words; again silence. The third time too none of us answered. Then he said, rise, Hudhayfah, bring us news of the enemy camp. After he called me by my name, I had no choice but to rise. He said, go, bring me news, but do not startle them against me. As I went away from him, it felt as if I were walking through a hot bath, until I reached them. I saw Abu Sufyan warming his back at the fire. I set an arrow on the bow and wanted to shoot; but I remembered the words of the Prophet {{3}}, do not startle them; had I shot, it would surely have hit; but I came back, and again it felt as if I were walking through a hot bath.{{4}}
blocks.7: Just then Abu Sufyan stood in the darkness of the night and said, O Quraysh, we cannot hold out here; the horses and camels are dying, Banu Qurayzah too did not keep their word, and this storm has thrown everything of ours into chaos; go back. Then he himself mounted his camel and set off, and the rest slipped away one by one.{{1}}
blocks.8: Hudhayfah (RA) went back and gave the Prophet {{1}} the whole report. As soon as the reporting was over he suddenly felt the cold; the Prophet {{2}} wrapped around him a part of the cloak in which he himself used to pray. He slept until morning. In the morning the Prophet {{3}} called, get up, sleepyhead.{{4}}
blocks.9: Three times he called and no one responded; only after being called by name did one stand up. Fear is human; but when called by name, that same person can walk calmly through the midst of the enemy camp. The Prophet {{1}} used to say afterwards,
blocks.11: There is no god but Allah, alone; He honoured His soldiers, helped His servant, and alone defeated the Confederates; after Him there is nothing.{{1}}
blocks.12: By morning the enemy camp was seen to be empty. Without a sword swung, without an arrow shot, a whole army had slipped away into the darkness of the night. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.14: From now on we will attack them, and they will not attack us; it is we who will march toward them.{{1}}
blocks.15: As soon as a defensive war had ended, the Prophet {{1}} declared, no more defence after this, now it is the turn of attack. After the Trench, Madinah was never attacked in this way again. In this siege of nearly a month only six Companions were martyred on the Muslim side; there is some variation in the narrations about the number of the enemy’s dead.{{2}}
blocks.16: The siege that was won without any sword fighting still had loss of life; war is never entirely without cost, yet the cost of this war was astonishingly low.
blocks.18: After the enemy left, the Prophet {{1}} laid down his weapons and sat down to bathe. Just then Jibril (AS) came.
blocks.20: Have you laid down your weapons? By Allah, we have not laid them down yet. Go out toward them. The Prophet {{1}} asked, where? He pointed toward Banu Qurayzah.{{2}}
blocks.21: The war that had seemed to be over was in fact not yet over. Banu Qurayzah had broken the pact at the Muslims’ most dangerous moment; the reckoning of that betrayal remained. Anas (RA) used to say, I can still seem to see the dust rising in the lane of Banu Ghanm, the dust of Jibril’s army, when the Prophet {{1}} set out toward Banu Qurayzah.{{2}}
blocks.22: The Prophet {{1}} asked for a volunteer to bring news from the enemy camp. al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam (RA) responded. He asked again, al-Zubayr (RA) responded again. The third time too it was the same. The Prophet {{2}} said,
blocks.24: Every prophet has a hawari, a devoted helper; my hawari is al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam.{{1}}
blocks.25: Hudhayfah (RA) had to be called by name, only then did he get up. In al-Zubayr’s (RA) case there was never any need to call; each time he raised his hand first. Fear does not lift in everyone the same way, some need to be called by name, some do not; yet both in the end stepped forward. The Prophet {{1}} announced that no one should pray ‘Asr before reaching Banu Qurayzah. The huge army was then moving strung out along the road, not everyone was in one place together. On the way, the time of ‘Asr came for one group. Some said, we will pray when we get there, as was said; some said, no, he did not mean this, let us pray on the way. The matter did not reach the Prophet {{2}} at that moment, was not settled at that moment; later, when he was informed, he blamed no one.{{3}}
blocks.26: The same command, two kinds of understanding; both sincere, both reasonable. The Prophet {{1}} told no one they were wrong, because the real goal was to arrive quickly, not to follow it letter by letter. When there is honesty in the effort to understand, even a differing view becomes tolerable. On reaching the fortress the Prophet {{2}} told the Companions to hold up shields and stand around him, so that his voice would carry clearly into the fortress. Then he called out, O brothers of monkeys and pigs! Surprised, they replied, O Abu al-Qasim, you never used to speak obscenely.{{3}}
blocks.27: The tribe that broke the pact at the Muslims’ most dangerous moment now has its fortress surrounded; the time has come to settle the reckoning of betrayal.
blocks.29: Before surrendering, Ka‘b ibn Asad, the leader of Banu Qurayzah, laid out three paths to his community. He said, come, let us accept Muhammad; by Allah, it has become clear to you too that he is a true prophet, the one who is written of in your own Book. They said, we will never abandon the law of the Torah. Ka‘b said, then come, let us kill our wives and children with our own hands, then fall upon Muhammad and his companions sword in hand; if we die, we die, leaving no burden behind. They said, kill these helpless people? What is the use of living without them? Ka‘b said, then let us attack tonight, Saturday night; Muhammad will not think that we would do anything on this night. They said, spoil the Sabbath? Have you forgotten what came upon our forefathers? Ka‘b said, from the day you were born from your mothers’ wombs, you have not been firm of purpose for even one night.{{1}}
blocks.30: Ka‘b had admitted with his own mouth that the truth had become clear to them. Yet instead of bowing before that truth, they chose one path of destruction after another, even to killing their own children with their own hands. To know the truth and refuse it out of pride is the greatest loss; the danger that could have been avoided with one acknowledgement became in the end inevitable. In the end they summoned their old ally Abu Lubabah (RA) and asked his advice. Seeing him, the women and children broke into tears. They asked, would it be right to submit to Muhammad’s decision? Abu Lubabah (RA) said yes with his mouth, but with his hand pointed to his throat, indicating that it meant killing. As soon as he had said it, he realised, before his feet had even moved from that place he understood, that he had betrayed Allah and His Messenger. He went to the mosque and tied himself to a pillar, saying, I will not move from here until Allah accepts my repentance.{{1}}
blocks.31: A man, realising his mistake, punished himself, before returning to Allah. This very honesty in admitting a mistake has kept him in history. After a siege of twenty-five days Banu Qurayzah surrendered, on one condition, that they would accept the decision of Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA). Sa‘d (RA) was still bedridden with the wound from the arrow.{{1}}
blocks.33: The people of Banu Qurayzah came down agreeing to Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh’s judgment. The Prophet {{1}} sent for Sa‘d, and he came riding a donkey. When he came near the mosque the Prophet {{2}} said to the Ansar, rise toward your chief, or your best man. Then it was said, these have come down agreeing to your judgment. He said, then I judge that their fighters be killed, and their children be taken captive. The Prophet {{3}} said, you have judged according to the command of Allah; sometimes he used to say, according to the command of the King.{{4}}
blocks.34: A wounded man, brought from his bed, yet both sides placed their trust in his decision. The weight of justice does not depend on bodily strength; it depends on conscience. This judgment coincided with the law of Banu Qurayzah’s own Torah, concerning a hostile tribe. Sa‘d (RA) showed no partiality even against the old allies of his own tribe; he decided on the path of justice.{{1}}
blocks.35: The Qur’an has described this fate of Banu Qurayzah like this,
blocks.37: Those of the People of the Book who had aided them (that is, the enemies of the Muslims), Allah made them come down from their fortresses and cast such fear into their hearts that you were killing some of them and taking some captive. Allah made you heirs to their land, their houses and their wealth, and to a land on which you had not yet set foot. Allah has power over all things.{{1}}
blocks.38: The verse also spoke of the land where no foot had yet been set. About two years after the fall of Banu Qurayzah, Khaybar came into Muslim hands; a promise whose fulfilment had to wait for time. It is hard to believe Allah’s promise exactly when its proof is not yet visible to the eyes; but that very time of waiting is the real test of faith. As soon as the judgment was over, Sa‘d’s (RA) wound began to bleed afresh. Soon after, he attained martyrdom. The Prophet {{1}} himself said that at his death the Throne of Allah shook, the doors of heaven were opened, and seventy thousand angels witnessed his funeral.{{2}}
blocks.39: At the burial the Prophet {{1}} was sitting beside the grave. Suddenly he recited tasbih twice, and everyone recited tasbih with him. Then he said takbir twice, and everyone said takbir. The Companions asked, O Messenger of Allah, what happened? He said,
blocks.41: The grave pressed upon this righteous servant so tightly that Allah later widened it for him.{{1}}
blocks.44: There is a squeezing in the grave; if anyone were to be saved from it, Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh would have been saved.{{1}}
blocks.45: He at whose death the Throne shook, at whose funeral seventy thousand angels bore witness, even his grave was not spared the first blow. Even the person of the greatest rank is not above reckoning; in Allah’s sight the reckoning is the same, the difference lies only in mercy.
blocks.47: From this dars of the fifth year of the Hijrah some pictures remain. A proposal of Salman (RA), which changed even the Arabs’ way of war. Two stones on the belly of the Prophet {{1}}, where the Companions had one each. Jabir’s (RA) one sa‘ of barley and a kid, with which several hundred people were fed. ‘Ali’s (RA) single combat, which gave the army of ten thousand its first shock. Safiyyah’s (RA) courage with a stick in hand, which protected a whole fortress. Nu‘aym’s (RA) three journeys, which broke an alliance of ten thousand without any sword. Sa‘d’s (RA) wounded body, yet one whose decision both sides trusted. And the greatest picture is the Prophet’s {{2}} own, carrying earth himself with a body smeared in mud, the hungriest of all yet first to get to work. So take one deed home from today’s dars.
blocks.49: While digging the trench the Prophet {{1}} tied two stones to his belly out of hunger, where the Companions had tied one each; in the share of hardship he was before everyone, in the share of comfort after everyone. Today I will ask myself a question: do I always make sure of my own share first, or have I ever learned to give others from my own share? Today I will give a little from my own plate of food to someone whom people do not usually ask after; I will not give up this small habit from today.

footnotes.1: Sahih Muslim 1788 (Kitab al-Jihad wa al-Siyar, Bab Ghazwat al-Ahzab; from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (RA), through Ibrahim al-Taymi ← his father Yazid ibn Sharik).
footnotes.2: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat al-Khandaq’ (Abu Sufyan’s announcement and return). Sirah-based.

footnotes.10: Sahih al-Bukhari 4119 (from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (RA)). From the two expressions ‘ba‘duhum’ (some of them) and ‘fa-dhukira dhalika li-l-Nabiyy {{1}}’ (the matter was reported to the Prophet {{2}}, in the passive voice, who reported it is unspecified) in the original Arabic text of the hadith it is understood that the matter was not settled in his direct presence, he was informed afterwards. ⚠ The text of the hadith contains no account of troop numbers or who was where; the statement ‘the army was strung out along the road’ in the dars is only a reasonable inference drawn from these two expressions, not a direct statement of the hadith. In the first draft a specific troop number (3,000, which is actually the figure for the opening moment of the Trench, not of this expedition) and an additional assumption that ‘the Prophet {{3}} was in the front group’ had been placed by mistake; they were caught in re-verification and removed.

There is real disagreement among muhaddithun about the chain of this narration; some have called it weak, and the words of the reply too have come differently through different sources (in one place ‘lam takun fahhashan’, that is, you were never foul-mouthed, in another ‘ma kunta jahulan’, that is, you never behaved like an ignorant person). In the dars the translation of the first narration (‘lam takun fahhashan’) has been used. There is also discussion among scholars explaining it, since such harsh language may seem contrary to the Prophet’s {{1}} natural gentleness. In the dars it is used only as a scene, not as an independent proof.

Imam al-Albani (may Allah have mercy on him) called this hadith sahih, and included it in both Sahih Sunan al-Nasa’i and Sahih al-Jami‘. In another narration of the same event (Ibn Ishaq, through several unnamed narrators) it is reported that Jibril (AS) came at night wearing a brocade turban and announced Sa‘d (RA)’s death; this part is weak in chain and was not used in the dars.
footnotes.20: Musnad Ahmad 24663 (from ‘A’ishah (RA), with the chain Shu‘bah ← Sa‘d ibn Ibrahim ← Nafi‘ ← an unnamed man ← ‘A’ishah (RA)). quiz.q: Whom did the Prophet ﷺ send on the stormy night to bring news of the enemy camp?
o: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (RA)
‘Ali (RA)
‘Umar (RA)
Sa‘d ibn Mu‘adh (RA) himself

quiz.q: Why was the storm called ‘only a means’?
o: The same kind of wind destroyed ‘Ad and helped the Muslims
That storm in reality had no real effect at all
Because there is no scientific explanation of the storm
It is merely the language of poets
quiz.e: In the light of Sahih al-Bukhari 4105.

quiz.q: Why did Hudhayfah (RA) not shoot Abu Sufyan with the arrow?
o: The Prophet’s ﷺ instruction was not to startle them
No arrow at all remained in the quiver then
He feared missing the target
He could not recognise Abu Sufyan in the dark

quiz.q: What can be learned about the mindset in times of danger from the storm incident?
o: No danger ever passes by itself
The power of nature is the greatest
Allah’s help can come even by unexpected paths
Human effort is really meaningless

quiz.q: Why did the Prophet ﷺ blame no one over the two understandings about the ‘Asr prayer?
o: The matter was not important to him at all
Both understandings were sincere and reasonable
He could not judge for lack of time
He only wanted to keep everyone happy

quiz.q: What can be applied from accepting two honest understandings of the same command?
o: All differences are really wrong, only one correct view should exist
The leader’s command should be kept unclear
If a command is not understood, it is better to ignore it
One can be tolerant of any difference of opinion held with an honest intention

quiz.q: How many proposals did Ka‘b ibn Asad give his community?
o: Two
Three
Four
Five

quiz.q: What did Abu Lubabah (RA) signal with his hand?
o: Toward the sky, a hint of mercy
Toward the fortress, a hint of surrender
Toward the throat, a hint of killing
Toward the sword, a hint of war

quiz.q: Why is it important that Sa‘d’s judgment matched the law of the Torah?
o: Banu Qurayzah were especially pleased with this judgment
It was merely a coincidental match
It proves he did not show partiality for old alliances
The Islamic ruling was changed by it

quiz.q: Why did Abu Lubabah (RA) tie himself to the pillar of the mosque?
o: Because the Prophet ﷺ himself had given him this punishment
Regretting, taking his own signal as betrayal
Because the people of Banu Qurayzah had forcibly kept him captive
Because he had been wounded in the war

quiz.q: What can be learned about justice from Sa‘d’s impartial judgment?
o: Justice should not be swayed by old relationships
A judge will always rule in favour of his own tribe
One should not judge while wounded
The judgment on an enemy must always be the harshest

quiz.q: What can be learned today from Abu Lubabah’s admission of his mistake?
o: When one errs it is better to hide it
Once one has erred there is no way back
On realising a mistake one should admit it with honest courage
Pointing out others’ mistakes is the most important thing
quiz.e: A lesson from Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Kathir.
